extracted.intended_audience: health sciences students, faculty, and researchers using PubMed (Des Moines University community)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether citations found via PubMed/Medline are peer-reviewed and how to handle possible non–peer-reviewed or predatory entries. Focused on using PubMed search results safely for biomedical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medline/PubMed citations are usually peer-reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the journals in Medline/PubMed are peer-reviewed. Generally speaking, if you find a journal citation in Medline/PubMed you should be just fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat presence in Medline/PubMed as a strong indicator of peer review, but not an absolute guarantee; use other checks when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: No PubMed filter to exclude non-referred titles
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no way to limit your results within PubMed to knock out the few publications that are not considered referred titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users cannot rely on a built-in PubMed filter to remove non-peer-reviewed items, so manual verification or secondary checks are needed for critical uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: PubMed includes citations from sources that may lack peer review (PubMed Central and NIH Preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PubMed interface contains citations from PubMed Central and the NIH Pre-prints, two sources of citations that contain journal publications or articles which have not met peer review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a record originates from PubMed Central or the NIH preprint collection, explicitly check the item for peer-review status (e.g., journal version, publication history) before treating it as peer-reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that predatory journals may be indexed
rubrics_metrics.description: There is concern within the scholarly community that predatory journal titles have found their way into citation databases like Pubmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume indexation guarantees legitimacy. Consult literature on the issue (e.g., Duc NM et al., 'Predatory Open Access Journals are Indexed in Reputable Databases') and evaluate journals for standard markers of legitimacy (editorial board, peer-review policies, publisher reputation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult a librarian if unsure about a title
rubrics_metrics.description: Please ask a librarian for help if you are concerned about a specific title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact library staff for verification and assistance evaluating suspect journals or articles; the page provides library contact info and encourages users to seek help.
